title: The House
mood: Lesley wakes from an old dream, and the ache behind her visor takes her back to the house where she grew up.

hero.alt: Lesley at night, seen from behind with her long gold hair over her face, lifts a gloved hand to the visor over her eye; beyond her the city lights glow under drifting embers.

segs.t: Down the corridor, Lesley was asleep in her chair.

She had left the pudding at the lab door, come back and gone on with the bolt. She had fallen asleep at it. The rifle lay across her knees, its bolt drawn back. The cleaning cloth was still in her hand, and the new coil lay on the cot where Chang’e had set it.
In her sleep, the old sounds came.
Screams and crying. Metal scraping on metal. Under it ran the roar of the Enders, and it never stopped for breath. She was running the wrong way through a crowd.
It was a familiar dream. It ended, every time, on a child’s voice.
“Go away! Leave me alone!”
Lesley woke. The cloth hit the floor, and her right hand had closed on the grip.
The room was dark and empty. Her cheeks were cold. She touched them, and her fingers came away wet.
Again.
The dream never reached back as far as the house she grew up in. The house came after, with the ache.
She did what she always did after the dream. She touched the visor over her left eye. The eye behind it lit, and a recording from years ago opened in the dark.
In it, Chang’e stood barely up to Lesley’s waist, beaming. She set something in Lesley’s palm: an eye, with a teal light in its middle.
“Happy Birthday, Lesley!”
Then Lesley bent down. The girl rose on her tiptoes, and two small hands pressed Lesley’s cheeks. They had been warm. Lesley remembered that.
Lesley watched it to the end.
The recording folded away. Behind the visor, where her own eye had been, the ache began. It took her back to the house.
Terrinia, 983.
The house ticked.
It stood on a narrow street of repair shops that ran downhill to the bay. Each shop had a bench in its window and someone at the bench, mending something.

Her father mended small machines, mostly clocks. They hung on every wall of the shop, each one out of step with the next. So the house ticked, day and night. As far as Lesley knew, it was the whole world.
Lesley stood on a crate to see over his bench. He let her hold the parts.
“The small one,” he said. “No, the smaller one.”
She held it up. “The pin.”
“Good.”
She learned the name of each part, so he would say “Good” again.
A clock on the bench would not start at all. He turned the key in its back. It still would not start.
“Don’t sulk,” her father told it.
Her mother laughed from the kitchen door. “He says that to all of them,” she told Lesley.
The four of them ate at one table in the kitchen. The biggest piece went to whoever had had the worst day. Her mother decided who that was.
One night there was pie. “Worst day?” asked her mother.
“Me,” said her little brother.
“You had a nap,” said Lesley.
“It was a bad nap.”
He got the piece.
Her mother kept one candle stub in the kitchen drawer. On a birthday she lit it on whatever there was. Once it was a boiled egg.
“Wish fast,” her mother told Lesley. “And wish small. It’s a small candle.”
Lesley wished for a bigger candle, and said so. Her mother kissed the top of her head and called her sensible. Then they blew it out quickly, so it would last.
On Lesley’s last birthday, her father had made her a bird out of tin. When she turned the key in its back, it hopped across the table and clicked its beak.
“It eats nothing,” said her father, “and it never sulks.”
She wound it eleven times before supper. After that it lived on the sill by her bed, where she would see it first thing.
Her brother followed her from room to room. He was too small to climb the crate, so he stood beside it and held on to Lesley’s leg. She was Sis to him. He never called her anything else.
Once, when they crossed to the baker’s, a cart came down the hill too fast. His hand went inside hers and squeezed.
“You’re squashing,” said Lesley.
He squeezed harder until the cart had gone by.

The first time Lesley heard the word Enders, it came out of the radio on her father’s bench. A man said they had been seen again, so far away it was past the edge of the map. Giants, he said. They came in groups and broke cities.
Her father turned the radio down.
To Lesley it sounded like a story. Giants were in stories. So were places past the edge of the map.
That night her brother would not sleep.
“Sis. Are Enders real?”
“Only in stories.”
“What if one comes?”
Lesley thought about it. She was the oldest. That was what the oldest was for.
“Then I’ll stand in front,” she said.
He fell asleep holding her sleeve.

After that he asked every night, and every night she said it. Her father began leaving the radio on in the shop at night, very low. He said it was for the weather. Her mother left the hall lamp on, so the dark would not come under the door.
One wet night he asked again.
“Sis. What if one comes?”
“Then I’ll stand in front.”
He held her sleeve and slept. Rain ran down the window. Lesley was nearly asleep, listening to it and to the clocks, when the radio downstairs stopped in the middle of a word.
The light under the door was gone. The house was dark.
The clocks her father wound by hand were still ticking. Then they struck one o’clock, all out of step.
Lesley climbed onto the sill. Down the hill, every street was dark. On the next hill, the last lights were going out one street at a time.
Over the bay hung a black cloud. Violet light moved inside it. Something was in there, too big for any cloud.
Only in stories,
she thought.
The tin bird stood on the sill. She turned its key, to see if it still worked. It hopped and clicked against the glass.
Her father was in the doorway. He had no light.
“Lesley. Off the sill.”
Her mother came up the stairs behind him with the birthday candle, lit, one hand cupped around the flame.
“It isn’t a birthday,” said her brother. He was sitting up in bed.
“No,” said her mother. “It’s for seeing.”
Lesley climbed down and sat beside him.
“Stay there,” said her father. “Both of you. The street is worse.”
Then the roar came. It came up the street from the bay, and the floor shook with it. After it came the screaming.
The wall went all at once. Rain blew in where it had been, and the candle went out.
A tall gray shape stood in the violet light. Its head was higher than the roof. It bent toward the bed.
In front. I said in front.
Lesley stepped in front of her brother. Something struck the left side of her face, and that side went dark.
At first it was only hot.
“Sis?” he said, behind her.
His fingers found her sleeve, the way they did every night. She reached back and closed her hand over them.
From the doorway her father shouted her name. Her mother reached past him, one hand out toward the bed. They were coming.
The roof came down.
Rain on her face woke her. The sky above her was gray. It was morning, and there was no roof.
Boards and plaster lay on top of her. She pushed until they moved, then pushed again.
Her left eye would not open. When she touched it, her hand came away red, and the rain washed it clean.
She called for each of them in turn. She called until her voice went thin. Nobody answered.
Under a beam she found her brother’s hand. She held it the way she held it crossing the street. It did not hold on.
I stood in front,
she thought.
I did.
Her father lay where the doorway had been. Her mother lay beside him, one hand still out toward the bed.
Lesley sat down in the rain between them. For a long time she did not get up.
When she could stand again, she went through what was left of the house.
She looked for the tin bird, and then for anything at all. Somewhere under the beams a clock was still ticking. She could not find that either.
There was nothing she could carry.
Down the hill, smoke rose through the rain from every house on the street. Lesley stood in it with her empty hands at her sides.
Next time,
she thought,
I won’t wait for one to come.
“I’ll kill them,” she told the smoke, out loud. “Every last Ender.”
The rain kept on. She said it again.
